newsitem.title: SWAZILAND: Swaziland could double sugar output in next decade.
newsitem.headline: Swaziland could double sugar output in next decade.

text.p: Swaziland could double its sugar output to a million tonnes a year in the next decade if an ambitious expansion plan proves successful, industry officials said.
With current sugar production at around 460,000 tonnes, the industry, which relies entirely on irrigation to grow sugarcane, plans to expand considerably in future.
"We could do a million tonnes given 10 years," Andy Colhoun, the general manager of the Swaziland Sugar Association told reporters on Thursday.
The country's sugarbelt is situated in what locals call "the Lowveld" close to the border with Mozambique and is the mainstay of the tiny mountain kingdom's economy.
Sugar contributes some 57 percent of Swaziland's foreign exchange earnings and accounts for 67 percent of agricultural production.
With lucrative preferential U.S. and European Union sugar quotas, Swaziland exports almost half of its raw sugar crop.
Lower labour and growing costs makes Swazi sugar cheaper than that produced by neighbouring South Africa and Swazi cane generally yielded more sucrose, Swazi officials said.
"Our problem is that we have not got enough sugar, we've got people queuing to come to Swaziland for our sugar," Colhoun said.
Recently, Swaziland did away with its old quota system to encourage new growers.
Colhoun said the system discouraged new growers who received a lower price for their cane than existing growers who only produced their allotted quota.
"People are now queuing to become new growers," he said.
Expansion plans included planting some 16,000 hectares more in the next ten years near two planned new dams -- Bovane dam in south eastern Swaziland and at Maguga dam in the northwest.
Work has already started on the Maguga dam infrastructure.
The industry said it would be able to cope with increased production.
"Sugarcane is useless unless you can process it. You can chew it but there is not a big market for chewing cane," Colhoun said.
Swaziland has three sugar mills with a capacity of over 500,000 tonnes a year and two refineries with a capacity of 90,000 tonnes of sugar each.
"There is enough milling capacity, (but) if we go over 600,000 to 700,000 tonnes we would have to build a fourth dam," Colhoun said.
But industry officials said Swazi expansion could worsen already strained relations with the South African Sugar Association (SASA).

The South African industry, claiming that imports of Swazi sugar were causing it to lose 275 million rand a year, denied Swaziland use of the sugar export terminal in Durban port, research and training facilities.
Swazi officials said they would only return to the negotiating table if SASA restored access to the facilities. --Johannesburg newsroom, 27-11 482 1003
